item.title: Manufacturing growth doubles to 3.2% amid easing cost pressures
item.description: By Yinka Kolawole Nigeria’s manufacturing sector recorded a 3.2 per cent year-on-year (YoY) growth in the second quarter of 2026, up from 1.6 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025, reflecting improved industrial activity amid gradual easing of operating pressures. The performance, according to data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), indicates a gradual recovery in the sector, supported by stronger activities across food and beverages, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, cement and refining subsectors. The improvement was also driven by relative stability in the foreign exchange market, which enhanced manufacturers’ access to imported raw materials and other production inputs, allowing businesses to improve procurement and inventory planning. Similarly, easing inflationary pressures helped reduce uncertainty around input costs, providing some relief to manufacturers and supporting production and business planning. The growth underscores manufacturing’s continued importance to Nigeria’s economic diversification efforts, particularly its role in expanding non-oil production, creating jobs and strengthening domestic value chains. However, despite the improved performance, manufacturers continue to contend with structural challenges, including high energy costs, inadequate infrastructure, logistics bottlenecks and elevated financing costs. These constraints have continued to undermine competitiveness, limit investment capacity and slow production expansion across several industrial segments. The moderation in inflation is expected to provide further relief to businesses and households, potentially supporting consumer demand and enabling manufacturers to plan production more effectively. Nevertheless, persistent geopolitical tensions in the Middle East remain a source of concern for the sector, given their potential implications for global energy prices and supply chains. Any escalation could trigger higher crude oil and gas prices, increase transportation and production costs, and reverse some of the gains from easing domestic inflationary pressures. For Nigerian manufacturers, sustaining the growth momentum will therefore depend not only on macroeconomic stability but also on addressing persistent structural constraints, particularly energy supply, infrastructure deficits and access to affordable financing. Onyema made a strong case for the harmonisation of tax regimes to promote fair competition and sustainability, particularly for private and charter airline operators. The Tax Ombud/Chief Executive, Dr. John Nwabueze, said the mandate of his Office includes promoting fairness, transparency and accountability in Nigeria’s tax administration system. He commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, for pioneering the establishment of the Office of the Tax Ombud, which is mandated to address operational, administrative and procedural grievances relating to taxes, levies, regulatory fees and customs duties. Nwabueze emphasised that the services of the Office are free of charge to Nigerians, providing an impartial platform for resolving disputes through mediation rather than adversarial proceedings. He further explained that the Office does not determine substantive tax liabilities but focuses on addressing gaps in complaint management and promoting voluntary compliance by building trust between taxpayers and revenue authorities. Underscoring the importance of stakeholder collaboration involving taxpayers, professional associations, business organisations, civil society and the media, he encouraged participants to share their experiences candidly and offer constructive recommendations. Nwabueze, who commended the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, for his leadership in tax reforms, reassured participants of the Office’s independence and commitment to resolving complaints promptly, reiterating its guiding principle of “bridging differences and building trust.” Engr. Olusola Obadimu, Director-General of the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA), described the Town Hall Meeting as a vital platform for addressing the persistent challenges confronting businesses and industries, ranging from inadequate infrastructure and rising energy costs to the increasing burden of taxation. Obadimu expressed support for the role of the Tax Ombud and commended Dr. Nwabueze for facilitating open dialogue between government and private-sector stakeholders. He called on policymakers to prioritise expanding the business landscape and supporting entire economic ecosystems, pledging NACCIMA’s collaboration with the Tax Ombud in promoting an equitable business environment conducive to enterprise growth and national development. Speaking on behalf of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN), Mr. Adewale Taju Olayinka emphasised that a fair and trustworthy tax system is fundamental to voluntary compliance and sustainable national revenue generation. Olayinka welcomed the establishment of the Office of the Tax Ombud as an important step towards strengthening accountability in tax administration and reaffirmed ICAN’s commitment to collaborating with the Office on professional capacity-building and taxpayer education. Delivering a goodwill message on behalf of the Association of National Accountants of Nigeria (ANAN), Mr. Bernard Akinnola underscored the importance of an equitable and predictable tax system, particularly amid ongoing reforms aimed at strengthening transparency and fiscal sustainability. He outlined five core principles that ANAN believes should underpin Nigeria’s tax administration system: transparency, equity, respect for taxpayer rights, professionalism and stakeholder collaboration. Dr. Titilayo Fowokan, speaking on behalf of the President of the Chartered Institute of Taxation of Nigeria (CITN), described the Tax Ombud as a landmark institutional innovation in Nigeria’s tax administration framework, with the potential to strengthen accountability, protect taxpayer rights and promote transparent grievance resolution. She noted that CITN considers the independent platform essential to building taxpayer confidence and fostering constructive relationships between taxpayers and revenue authorities. Fowokan reaffirmed CITN’s commitment to supporting the Tax Ombud’s mandate and promoting high professional standards in tax administration. Speaking on behalf of the Executive Director of the Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC), Arc. Benedict Itegbe commended the Office of the Tax Ombud for extending its stakeholder engagement to Lagos. He noted that free and impartial mechanisms for seeking redress are crucial to promoting a competitive non-oil export sector. Itegbe urged exporters to maintain comprehensive records and take advantage of the avenues provided by the Tax Ombud to address complaints relating to unfair treatment and complex tax-compliance challenges. He assured the Office of NEPC’s readiness to promote awareness of its services, support systemic improvements and sustain collaboration in bridging gaps between taxpayers and revenue authorities. Mr. Olufemi Adewole, representing the Depot and Petroleum Products Marketers Association of Nigeria (DAPPMAN), highlighted the significant operational and fiscal challenges confronting oil and gas marketers, particularly delays in VAT refunds and high working-capital costs. He acknowledged the government’s revenue-generation needs but stressed that taxation should not contribute to escalating the cost of living. He therefore advocated regular reviews of fiscal policies affecting petroleum marketers to assess their impact on downstream operations. Prince Olusegun Oduntan, National Vice President, Association of Nigerian Licensed Customs Agents (ANLCA) highlighted concerns over personal taxes, local government levies for various amenities, and the method of taxing based on total turnover rather than actual profit margins. He emphasized the association’s intention to submit a detailed position paper to the Office of the Tax Ombud, seeking redress and more equitable tax assessment practices tailored to the realities of their business model. The Town Hall Meeting was attended by representatives of the Nigerian Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (NASME), National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW), Nigerian Association of Small Scale Industrialists (NASSI), Nigeria Network of NGOs (NNNGO), Nigeria Employers’ Consultative Association (NECA), Lagos Hotel Owners and Managers Association, Association of Nigerian Licensed Customs Agents, Petroleum and Natural Gas Senior Staff Association of Nigeria (PENGASSAN), and Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) among others. item.title: Without manufacturing $1tr economy is an illusion
item.description: By Dele Sobowale Japan in fact offers a relevant historical example of what can happen to an economy which falls behind in the global manufacturing race. Even in Africa, the Giant of Africa is lagging behind at least three other economies in the scale and scope of manufacturing. Consequently, the politically-motivated promise to make Nigeria a one trillion dollar economy by 2030 is only one of the many illusions of the Tinubu administration. Desirable as it is, a $1 trillion economy is unachievable for reasons too numerous to discuss now, but, the cardinal reason is Nigeria’s weak manufacturing base – forcing us to import thousands of products which we can, with little effort, produce locally. I was a Senior Lecturer/Consultant working with the Nigerian Institute of Management, NIM, in 1992, when Morita wrote the article in which that statement was made. The NIM Library was my second home and office. When not busy teaching courses in Sales, Marketing and General Management, I was in the Library reading and gathering materials for my lectures, as well as my book of quotations, VBQ – which was published in 2007. Japan was the world’s second largest manufacturing economy as well as the second largest economy; and was threatening the American leadership in that regard. Several books were written on the Art of Japanese Management; leading American Business Schools included courses in Japanese business methods in their curricula as compulsory subjects. The Japanese economy was growing at 7 to 10 per cent annually; and projections were made regarding when it would overtake the US as the largest economy globally. I was a Senior Lecturer/Consultant working with the Nigerian Institute of Management, NIM, in 1992, when Morita wrote the article in which that statement was made. Several books were written on the Art of Japanese Management; leading American Business Schools included courses in Japanese business methods in their curricula as compulsory subjects. Nigeria Is Missing The Boat Once Again “Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” George Santayana, 1863-1952, VBQ p 93. It might be difficult for the Generation Z youths to believe that Nigeria once embarked on rapid industrialization. The Gowon administration sent delegations to the United States in 1974 to appeal to young and well-educated Nigerians to return home and fill vacant positions opening up in manufacturing in several industrial layouts in Lagos, Ibadan, Kaduna, Kano, Portharcourt and Aba. I was one of those who responded to the call to return home and help Nigeria’s transformation to a manufacturing giant. On arrival in August 1974, my first working experience was at the Ilupeju Industrial Layout in Lagos. I soon discovered there were others in Lagos State – Ikeja, Iganmu and Apapa. My first trip to Portharcourt and Aba revealed the Trans Amadi and Ogbor Hill layouts respectively; the Northern legs of the national familiarization tour took me to Kano’s Bompai, Kaduna and Anglo Jos in Plateau state. Granted, everything I saw could not have been more than a few establishments on Route 128, Massachusetts, USA – where I gained industrial experience. But it was a promising start. Construction of new factories and expansion of old factories was going on at feverish pace. Jobs were available everywhere. I left manufacturing enterprises in 1990 after working in five different industrial layouts. The last was in Kalambina, Sokoto State. Fourteen years later, the Federal Government is still offering the same excuses for remaining stuck at 4,000MW on a good day. No $1 trillion economy generates less than 45,000MW. South Africa is Africa’s largest economy, far less than the $1 trillion economy. But, it already provides more than 45,000MW. “Banks’ loan to manufacturers slumps 26.8% to N5.19trn.” VANGUARD, October 26, 2026. Credit is the soul of business and has been an axiom for several hundred years. Banks and financial institutions were established primarily to promote businesses; not to finance government deficits. The Great Depression in the last century, as well as the rise of Keynesianism, gave rise to governments invading banks to borrow funds for their operations. Deficit spending, once proposed as a short-term measure, has hardened into a permanent feature of fiscal policy. Very few governments now attempt to balance their budgets. item.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, November 16, 2026
item.description: The Nigerian naira opened Monday, November 16, 2026, under mild pressure across the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) while maintaining relative stability in the parallel market. At the official window, data published by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) shows the NFEM rate referencing ₦1,353.97 per dollar. This follows a ₦7.18 depreciation in the preceding session as corporate foreign exchange obligations and seasonal end-of-year import demand weighed on liquidity. Meanwhile, spot interbank indicators in early morning trading hovered around ₦1,343.35 per dollar as dealers awaited fresh intraday price discovery. In the parallel market, also known as the black market, Bureau De Change (BDC) operators and street dealers in Lagos and Abuja quoted the US dollar at a buying rate of ₦1,380 and a selling rate of ₦1,390. With the official rate standing at ₦1,353.97 and the parallel market selling at ₦1,390, the exchange rate spread between both markets sits at approximately ₦36.03 per dollar. Market analysts note that steady foreign reserve buffers and ongoing CBN market interventions continue to keep the disparity between the official and unofficial segments within a narrow band compared to historical volatility. item.title: Stock market rebounds as investors reap N2.2trn amid decline in oil price
item.description: By Peter Egwuatu The Nigerian stock market rebounded last week after weeks of sustained pressure from profit taking led to decline in stock value. Equity investors on the Nigerian Exchange Limited, NGX, last week, reaped over N2.2 trillion in capital gains leading the NGX market capitalisation, to close last week at N163.795 trillion, up from N161.593 trillion the previous week. Similarly, another major market performance indicator, NGX All Share Index, ASI, surged by 1.4 % to close at 252,269.16 points from 248,877.22 points the previous week, indicating renewed demand for selected heavyweight stocks, which dominated the market. Analysts noted that although buying interests remained evident in major banking and industrial stocks , the broader market reflected a mixed trading pattern, with investors maintaining selective positions amid intermittent profit-taking in several stocks The positive performance, according to analysts, highlights the continued resilience of the domestic stock market, which has maintained substantial gains since the beginning of the year. Reacting to market performance and outlook analysts at InvestData Consulting Limited, said : “ The immediate market outlook remains cautiously positive, supported by the strong year-to-date return and continued interest in selected large-cap stocks. Nevertheless, investors are likely to maintain a selective approach, considering corporate earnings, dividend expectations, valuation levels and prevailing macroeconomic conditions before increasing their exposure. The possibility of further profit-taking cannot be ruled out, particularly in stocks that have recorded significant gains in recent sessions. Overall, the market appears to be consolidating its recent advances while maintaining an underlying bullish bias. The ability of the index to break above the 255,000-point resistance level, alongside improved market participation, will be important in determining whether the current upward movement can extend into another phase of appreciation.” They further noted that the political outcome of the US midterm elections introduced additional uncertainty into the market adding that the developments have placed renewed attention on the possibility of diplomatic negotiations and their implications for global crude supply. “For Nigeria, the movement in international crude prices remains particularly important given the country’s dependence on oil exports for foreign exchange earnings and government revenue. A sustained decline in crude prices could place additional pressure on projected oil receipts, especially if production levels remain below expectations. Conversely, elevated prices could support external earnings, although the benefits would depend on domestic production performance, export volumes and fiscal management” the analysts added. For many market women who rely on interstate commercial buses and trucks to restock goods such as foodstuffs, textiles, and household provisions, waybill logistics are the lifeline of daily commerce. However, traders said the shrinking grace periods before daily demurrage charges kick in have turned routine restocking into a financial burden. Nigeria Is Missing The Boat Once Again “Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” – George Santayana, 1863-1952, VBQ p 93. It might be difficult for the Generation Z youths to believe that Nigeria once embarked on rapid industrialization. The Gowon administration sent delegations to the United States in 1974 to appeal to young and well-educated Nigerians to return home and fill vacant positions opening up in manufacturing in several industrial layouts in Lagos, Ibadan, Kaduna, Kano, Portharcourt and Aba. I was one of those who responded to the call to return home and help Nigeria’s transformation to a manufacturing giant. On arrival in August 1974, my first working experience was at the Ilupeju Industrial Layout in Lagos. I soon discovered there were others in Lagos State – Ikeja, Iganmu and Apapa. My first trip to Portharcourt and Aba revealed the Trans Amadi and Ogbor Hill layouts respectively; the Northern legs of the national familiarization tour took me to Kano’s Bompai, Kaduna and Anglo Jos in Plateau state. Granted, everything I saw could not have been more than a few establishments on Route 128, Massachusetts, USA – where I gained industrial experience. But it was a promising start. Construction of new factories and expansion of old factories was going on at feverish pace. Jobs were available everywhere. I left manufacturing enterprises in 1990 after working in five different industrial layouts. The last was in Kalambina, Sokoto State. Unfortunately, the 16 years between 1974 and 1990 represented the period of the rise and decline of manufacturing in Nigeria. Instead of building on what we started, gradual decline set in. SPARS, a retail outlet, has replaced our factory for analgesics and cough syrup. The brewery in Bompai lies in ruins; and the rice mill in Sokoto remains shut since 1991. Right now, the current reforms embarked upon by President Tinubu threaten to again set in motion the process which made manufacturing extremely difficult in Nigeria. Current Situation: No Power; Expensive Credit “Power supply plunges as gas shortage, water level worsen.” VANGUARD, November 6, 2026 Manufacturing became very attractive in the 1970s when the Kainji Hydro Power Station was established. None of the industrial estates could have been started without relatively reliable public power supply. Definitely, Nigerian Paper Mill, Jeba; Nigerian Sugar Company, NISUCO and the Nigerian Yeast and Alcohol Manufacturing Company, both at Bacita, Kwara State could not have been started if they had to operate on generators. I was a consultant for the three; and I recall the discussions with their Chief Executive Officers. Without exception, they were certain their companies could not survive on generators. They were absolutely correct. On November 5, 2026, Nigeria was able to supply only 2,926MW to the entire nation. That is deeply concerning for two reasons. One, we achieved capacity to generate 4,000MW per day as far back as 2012. Fourteen years later, the Federal Government is still offering the same excuses for remaining stuck at 4,000MW on a good day. No $1 trillion economy generates less than 45,000MW. South Africa is Africa’s largest economy, far less than the $1 trillion economy. But, it already provides more than 45,000MW. “Banks’ loan to manufacturers slumps 26.8% to N5.19trn.” VANGUARD, October 26, 2026. Credit is the soul of business and has been an axiom for several hundred years. Banks and financial institutions were established primarily to promote businesses; not to finance government deficits. The Great Depression in the last century, as well as the rise of Keynesianism, gave rise to governments invading banks to borrow funds for their operations. Deficit spending, once proposed as a short-term measure, has hardened into a permanent feature of fiscal policy. Very few governments now attempt to balance their budgets. Reliance on deficit spending and perpetual borrowing is the new normal. In the process, banks are increasingly called upon to extend credits to the government. Private sector borrowers, especially manufacturers are bearing the brunt of the new situation. Nigerian manufacturers are being hammered three ways. First, they don’t receive as much as they would want. Second, the interest rates are exorbitant. Third, they compete against foreign producers whose governments provide support across the board and whose banks charge single digit interest rates. How we expect Nigerian manufacturers paying 30 per cent to compete with Chinese paying 2 per cent remains a mystery to me. item.title: Igini to Trump: Tie Nigeria-US relations to credible polls
item.description: A former Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, Resident Electoral Commissioner, Mike Igini, has urged US President, Donald Trump, to link America’s immigration policy and diplomatic relations with Nigeria to credible conduct of the country’s 2027 general elections. Read Also: ‘How Tinubu will end insecurity ready’ Igini said electoral malpractice, corruption, insecurity and poor governance were among the factors forcing Nigerians to seek opportunities abroad, arguing that credible elections and accountable leadership could help address the root causes of migration. In an open letter dated November 13, 2026, and addressed to Trump at the White House, the former REC proposed a policy he called the “No Mandate Fraud” Doctrine, urging the US to combine preventive diplomacy, independent election monitoring and targeted sanctions against individuals involved in electoral violations. He argued that border enforcement alone could not address migration without tackling the governance failures driving Nigerians out of their country. “Nigerians are not leaving Nigeria because they do not love their country. They are leaving because of decades of persistent electoral malpractice, corruption, insecurity and weak public accountability that have undermined Nigerians’ confidence in government,” he wrote. Igini urged Trump to send a high-level delegation to engage President Bola Tinubu, political parties, presidential and governorship candidates, INEC and other relevant institutions ahead of the elections. He said the delegation should communicate Washington’s position that credible elections, peaceful political competition and respect for constitutional rights were central to US interests in Nigeria. He also proposed visa restrictions, financial sanctions and asset freezes, where legally justified, against electoral officials found culpable of manipulating results, falsifying records or committing other electoral offences. item.title: We demand impeccable voter register
item.description: The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, must urgently clean up its battered image by producing an impeccable voters’ register ahead of the 2027 general elections. The discovery that its own officials allegedly compromised the database through fraudulent registrations is a monumental embarrassment. It reinforces existing suspicions about the commission’s impartiality and competence at a time Nigerians desperately need an electoral umpire they can trust. The scale of the problem is alarming. Of the more than 11 million people registered during the 2026 Continuous Voter Registration, CVR, exercise, INEC’s Automated Biometric Identification System, ABIS, flagged approximately 1.5 million entries as suspicious. The commission subsequently removed 1,277,252 invalid records, leaving about 268,000 requiring further verification. The preliminary national register contains over 103.4 million voters. More disturbing is the alleged complicity of registration officers who abused their official login credentials to introduce fictitious identities. They reportedly uploaded AI-generated photographs, reused identical images and exploited registration provisions for persons with disabilities, claiming fictitious applicants had no fingers and could therefore bypass normal fingerprint verification. ABIS detected suspicious facial and biometric inconsistencies during screening. Artificial intelligence has consequently introduced a dangerous dimension toa electoral fraud. Its capacity to generate convincing human faces makes fabricating identities easier and visual inspection less reliable. Although digitally enhanced photographs of genuine applicants are not necessarily fraudulent, fictitious identities must be identified and eliminated. INEC says it has withdrawn implicated officers’ access credentials, commenced investigations, subjected suspicious entries to human adjudication and referred evidence for possible disciplinary action and prosecution. It promises further verification before the final register is displayed on December 15, 2026. These assurances are insufficient without demonstrable accountability. Public confidence in INEC was already fragile before this scandal. Controversies surrounding previous elections, particularly the disputed 2023 presidential election and the failure of IReV to upload results as expected, have deepened distrust. A manipulated register could facilitate fictitious voting identities, impersonation, inflated constituency figures and deliberate disenfranchisement of legitimate voters. The occasion embodied three primary characteristics of the seventy-eight-year-old ASUU. The second ASUU culture is ever interrogating the present, which is why this year’s theme focused on the electoral system. The third is the union’s tendency to probe into the future. This time, it looked at the ongoing attempts to create State Police and the possible impact it could have on the 2027 General Elections. ASUU is also quite strategic in building alliances, which is why its awardees this year included a number of people who led the Government Negotiating Teams or played roles in ensuring the success of the decades-long ASUU-Government negotiations. These included Alhaji Ahmed, Professor MunzaliJibril, whose Negotiating Team in May 2021 broke through barriers and successfully produced a draft agreement, and Professor NimiDimkpa Briggs, who, on June 16, 2022, despite government reservations, followed through with a new draft agreement within ten weeks. The Buhari government had been so displeased with the breakthrough the Briggs Team had made with ASUU that it made false accusations against the likeable professor. It accused him of excluding government agencies from the negotiations, inflating academics’ salaries by N1.1 trillion, and acting out of financial self-interest. In making the last two allegations, it escaped the government’s mind that Briggs had retired from service and, as such, would not be a beneficiary of the enhanced academics’ pay. When Briggs passed on ten months later, the same Buhari government praised him to high heavens for his dignity, truthfulness, and “historic contributions” to education. Alhaji Ahmed, speaking on behalf of the awardees, joked about his experience with ASUU President Chris Piwuna, a professor of psychiatry whom he said tried to make him his patient, but he rejected such negotiation tactics. He dedicated his award to former ASUU President and current Trustee, Professor AsisiAsobie, whom he said introduced him to the union’s unique ways of negotiation. Asobie, he said, would refuse to even drink water in his office because they were negotiating. Professor Piwuna, in analysing the situation in the country, said: “The Nigerian Universities and our members have suffered their share of violence and trauma. Some campuses were attacked; we have lost members across branches, and several students have been killed, staff displaced, and properties lost. Our universities have become theatres of ‘war’ and easy targets for insurgents, from Jos to Abuja, and campuses in North West Nigeria.” I had the honour of delivering the 2026 ASUU Annual Lecture titled: ‘Insecurity, Incumbency and Elections in Nigeria: The Role of State Police.’ I pointed out that in the past eleven years of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) administrations of Buhari and Tinubu, at least 97,111 persons have been killed in violent conflicts. Also, that Nigeria, in the 2026 Global Terrorism Index (GTI) Report, ranks fourth globally, trailing Pakistan, Burkina Faso, and Niger. I therefore submitted that even with the assistance of the military, the police are not coping with insecurity. I listed challenges of the police as including their inability to wean themselves of their colonial origins of relying on force, repression, and suppression of Nigerians rather than being a civil agency and a friend of the people. Other problems I mentioned are very poor remuneration and welfare and job insecurity, particularly amongst its top echelons. One of the suggestions I made was that, career-wise, the police should be run like the public service, where the promotion of a few as Permanent Secretaries or Head of Service does not mean all the Directors senior to them are sacked. In the alternative, that a non-policeman, such as a judge or senior lawyer, be made the Inspector General of Police (IGP). If a non-soldier can be the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, a non-policeman can be the IGP. These challenges, I posited, make the establishment of State Police necessary, especially when they will be recruited from locals familiar with the terrain and local culture. The fact that there will be multiple police agencies would not lead to administrative challenges, as the United States runs 17,985 police agencies and Canada, 160. The challenges I see include whether state governments that cannot pay workers’ salaries can afford State Police or whether governors who employ thugs would not recruit them into the State Police. Accusing fingers also point to Tinubu for making their own political parties unviable platforms for the two men. This leaves the African Democratic Congress (ADC), which faces the most crisis of all. For almost a year, the ADC, formed by a partial coalition of like-minded and opposition interests, has been held hostage by the antics of one man, enabled almost entirely by Nigerian courts. The status of ADC candidates, from the presidential to the state assembly elections, currently hangs in limbo because Nigerian courts in this era now think that the dubious concerns of one party member are more important than the will of all the voters in the hundreds of primary elections conducted by the APC in the past months. In short, Nigeria today looks like a one-party state, with the ruling APC as the last man standing. In my view, however, Nigeria is not sliding into a one-party state. It is already a one-man state. A one-party state—a country where a single political party dominates the political space—is a form of authoritarian rule, whether codified in law or in practical effect. In practice, however, there can be significant checks, political pressure and opposition within the ruling one party itself. More importantly, while undemocratic, one-party states tend to be developmental. They typically maintain political legitimacy through rapid industrialisation and all-round national development, as illustrated by the former Communist countries in Europe, including the defunct USSR, and most strikingly by today’s Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which lifted more than 600 million people out of acute poverty in under 30 years. Tinubu’s APC is nothing like a one-party state in this sense because the twin scaffolds of legitimacy—a serious national development agenda and internal checks—are wholly lacking. Instead, we have a president who straddles his party and the nation without any effective guardrails to his power. That is not a one-party state; it is, rather, a one-man state, whereby nearly all formal institutions of the state, all political parties, civil society, and other informal power brokers no longer provide any meaningful constraints on the will of the president. That is not good for Nigeria, and I am not sure it is something good for the President himself. Since 1999, Nigeria has never really had a true multi-party or two-party system, with the exception of the two-year period between 2013 and 2015. What we have always had is a pseudo-one-party state, whereby a single political party dominates the political space: first the PDP, from 1999 to 2013, and then the APC, during 2015–2023. But even during those years of pseudo-democracy, there were at least two important guardrails against presidential power that ensured that our democracy continued to grow and thrive. First, ruling party politics in Nigeria since 1999 was always characterised by significant political pressure and opposition within the party itself, even in the near absence of an effectively coordinated or strong opposition party. That pressure and opposition came from various factions of the ruling party, or from other centres of power within the party and government. Secondly, there was significant and effective opposition from outside the party and government, particularly from the media, labour unions and organised civil society. The result was that no president was able to win or get everything he wanted all the time. For example, former President Olusegun Obasanjo was the most powerful of Nigerian leaders from 1999 to 2023. But even at the peak of his power, Obasanjo still faced serious pressure and opposition from ruling party chairs, governors, members and leaders of the National Assembly, etc., many of whom frequently disagreed or clashed openly with him. Industrial strikes by unions were effective enough to compel the government to backtrack on some of its policies. Newspapers and civil society organisations were firm and stringent in their criticisms of presidential overreach. It was only natural, then, that Obasanjo’s third-term bid was defeated. Presidents Umar Yar’Adua, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari were all more or less the same, as significant power blocks within and outside the ruling party and government provided significant checks on their power. The Governors’ Forum was a powerful wedge on Yar’Adua, and, since 1999, the National Assembly was probably most assertive under Buhari’s first term. Governors Uzo Kalu of Abia and Attahiru Bafarawa of Sokoto fought tooth and nail against Obasanjo, not to mention Senate President Chuba Okadigbo, Speaker Ghali Na’Abba and even Dimeji Bankole, just as Governor Ortom screamed at Buhari daily for eight years. If for nothing else, these pressures were useful for defeating Obasanjo’s “third term”, for getting Yar’Adua to initiate enduring reforms in our electoral system, for the doctrine of necessity that made Jonathan President, for forcing Jonathan to accept defeat in the 2015 elections, and for making a democrat out of Buhari—all of which, and more, are important moments of progress in our democratic journey. But my broader point is that all of these guardrails of our developing democracy have been blown off, bought up or buried under the rubble of President Tinubu’s silent corrosion of Nigerian politics, economy and society, leaving us with something worse than a pseudo-one-party state: that is, a one-man state. The ruling APC itself, the National Assembly, the governors, including those pretending to belong to other parties, the courts, the anti-corruption agencies, large sections of the religious and traditional establishment, and equally large sections of the media and so-called “civil society” all appear to be answering to or doing the bidding of one man in Nigeria today. Only Nigerians and their date with INEC in January and February are now left standing. We will see. item.title: PenCom opens up on N52,000 minimum pension guarantee
item.description: By Victor Ahiuma-Young The National Pension Commission, PenCom, has shed light on the implementation of the long-awaited Minimum Pension Guarantee, MPG, disclosing that 173,209 Nigerian retirees are eligible to benefit from a guaranteed minimum monthly pension of N52,500 following its formal activation by President Bola Tinubu. The initiative, aimed at improving the welfare and financial security of retirees under the Contributory Pension Scheme, CPS, was unveiled alongside a healthcare programme designed to provide free access to essential medical services for low-income pensioners. The two initiatives, the Minimum Pension Guarantee and the Pension Industry Healthcare Plan (PenCare), were announced at the Presidential Pension Security Initiatives ceremony held at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja. Tinubu, who was represented at the event by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, said the Minimum Pension Guarantee fulfilled a provision of the Pension Reform Act 2004, which was retained in the 2014 legislation but had remained unimplemented for 22 years. Declaring the scheme operational, the President assured pension contributors that the government would no longer allow eligible retirees to receive pensions below the guaranteed minimum threshold. “From this day, there is a floor beneath the Nigerian retiree. No one who contributed under the Contributory Pension Scheme will ever be allowed to fall below,” he said.
